name: Physical sabotage and drone threats

points.name: Physical sabotage and drone threats

summary: No longer hypothetical. Drone strikes on three AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain in March 2026 moved geopolitical exclusion review from a theoretical underwriting question to a live one for Gulf-region operators, and the same wording reaches any site near contested airspace.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: A war exclusion that includes drone strikes by non state actors would remove cover for the exact March 2026 UAE and Bahrain losses.
A terrorism exclusion without a separate standalone terrorism buyback leaves no cover for politically motivated drone sabotage.
A malicious acts or sabotage exclusion that carves out damage caused by unmanned aerial vehicles defeats the core property damage claim.
A sublimit for physical damage caused by aircraft or drones of USD 250,000 would be inadequate for a destroyed data hall with tens of millions in equipment.
A contingent business interruption exclusion for power or telecommunications failure triggered by a drone strike on a nearby substation would leave operators without revenue cover.
A political risk exclusion that applies to any event in a designated conflict zone would exclude Gulf sites near contested airspace even if no active hostilities occur at the site.
A cyber exclusion that treats drone guidance system interference as cyber terrorism could deny a physical damage claim arising from a jammed or hijacked drone.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Negotiate a limited war and terrorism buyback endorsement that covers drone strikes by non state actors but excludes declared war between nation states.
Add a hostile acts clarification that physical damage from unmanned aerial vehicles is not excluded under the standard aircraft exclusion.
Carve back sabotage and malicious damage to include acts by persons not employed by the insured, with no drone specific sublimit.
Obtain a political risk exclusion amendment that removes blanket exclusion for the Gulf Cooperation Council region and instead applies only to sites within a defined radius of active hostilities.
Negotiate a contingent business interruption extension for loss of utilities caused by drone damage to off site power or telecommunications infrastructure.
Add a service interruption endorsement that covers loss of income when a drone strike damages a third party data centre that hosts the insured's cloud workloads.
Secure a 72 hour extended period of indemnity for physical damage from drone strikes to allow for debris removal and security upgrades before operations resume.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: Business interruption waiting periods for physical damage from drone strikes are commonly 24 to 72 hours, but some Gulf operators negotiate a 12 hour waiting period given single points of failure in power and connectivity.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Business interruption cover is typically written on a gross earnings basis with an indemnity period of 12 to 18 months, and extended to include contingent business interruption for loss of power or connectivity from a drone strike on a nearby substation.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Electronic data processing equipment is usually insured on a replacement cost basis with separate sublimits for servers, storage, and networking gear, often USD 100 million to USD 250 million per location.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: Per occurrence property limits are typically layered from USD 50 million primary up to USD 500 million or more in excess layers, with total insured values for a hyperscale campus often exceeding USD 1 billion.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: Primary commercial general liability limits for Gulf data centre operators are typically set by customer and landlord contracts, commonly between USD 5 million and USD 25 million per occurrence, with higher limits required for hyperscale tenants.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Occurrence based because a drone strike is a sudden and identifiable event, and third party bodily injury or property damage claims may be reported years after the physical damage occurs, making claims made wording unsuitable for this exposure.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess umbrella towers are layered above the primary in increments of USD 25 million to USD 100 million, with total tower height driven by contractual indemnity obligations to cloud providers and local regulatory requirements for critical infrastructure.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: A drone strike that causes fire or explosion can lead to bodily injury claims from employees, contractors, or emergency responders at the data centre.
Debris from a destroyed drone or damaged building can cause third party property damage to neighbouring buildings, vehicles, or public infrastructure.
Cloud tenants may bring breach of contract claims for service interruption if the operator fails to meet uptime commitments after a physical sabotage event.
The operator may face liability for failure to implement reasonable security measures if a court finds that drone detection systems were absent or inadequate.
Pollution liability can arise from burning servers, batteries, and diesel fuel released during a drone strike, triggering cleanup obligations to local authorities.
Evacuation and emergency response costs incurred by third parties, such as nearby businesses forced to close, may be claimed under a general liability theory of nuisance.

underwriter_wants_to_know: Underwriters will ask for the precise geographic coordinates of each data centre and its distance from known drone launch corridors or contested airspace in the Gulf region.
They will require details of physical perimeter security including drone detection radar, radio frequency jamming, and kinetic interception systems installed after the March 2026 AWS strikes.
They will ask for the redundancy architecture of power and cooling systems to assess whether a single drone strike on one facility can cascade into a regional outage.
They will request copies of customer service level agreements and any liquidated damages clauses that could convert a physical loss into a large contractual liability.
They will ask about the ownership and nationality of the operating entity because sanctions or export control restrictions may affect the availability of drone defence technology.
They will want to see the historical loss runs for any prior sabotage attempts, drone sightings, or perimeter intrusions at the site.
They will ask whether the insured has a formal business continuity plan that includes relocation of critical workloads to facilities outside the Gulf region.
